prompt: What is the defining failure of the PowerPoint architect?
hint: Lesson 2: a diagram is a view.

choices.text: Using slides instead of a proper modelling tool
choices.why: The tool is not the problem; a diagram drawn in any tool fails the same way if nobody ties it to the code.

choices.text: The drawing, not the system, is what gets looked at
choices.why: Right: the slides describe a system that exists nowhere else, and the code drifts away unnoticed.

choices.text: Drawing a target state for the system at all, however carefully
choices.why: Describing where the system should go is part of the job; the alternative keeps the target and adds a path.

choices.text: Presenting architecture to executives
choices.why: Executives need the picture too. The failure is that nobody in that room can check it against the code.

prompt: A new Payments engineer reads the architecture deck, builds a report on the "payment settled" event shown on slide 20, and learns after four days that the event was never built. Which antipattern produced the loss?
hint: Where does the event exist?

choices.text: Overengineering
choices.why: Nothing was built beyond the need; the trouble is a drawing of something that was not built at all.

choices.text: The ivory tower
choices.why: The tower is about deciding without the teams; here the decision may have been fine and the drawing is false.

choices.text: The PowerPoint architect
choices.why: Right: a decision taken on a picture of a system that exists only on the slide.

choices.text: The absent architect, since nobody built the event
choices.why: There was an architect, drawing a great deal; the drawing was not tied to the code.

prompt: Which change turns a target-architecture slide into something the PowerPoint architect would not have produced?
hint: A target with no first step is a wish.

choices.text: Adding more detail to every box on the slide
choices.why: More detail on a drawing nobody checks against the code makes it more convincing, not more true.

choices.text: A first step owned by a team, with a date
choices.why: Right: the target becomes a sequence of shippable steps, starting from the system as it is.

choices.text: Presenting it again each quarter to the executives
choices.why: Repeating it to the same audience, who cannot check it, changes nothing about its distance from the code.

choices.text: Moving it from slides to a diagram tool with a version history
choices.why: A history of the drawing is not a link to the code; the fix is a path and a check, not a new file format.

prompt: A company hires 15 engineers a year, and each loses 4 days building against a component that exists only in the architecture deck. How many days a year does the deck cost?
hint: Hires times days lost.

prompt: Why does the lesson count a fitness function as part of the alternative to the PowerPoint architect?
hint: What happens the day the code disagrees with it?

choices.text: It replaces diagrams, so nothing is drawn any more
choices.why: The alternative keeps drawing; the check covers the rules a machine can read.

choices.text: It produces slides automatically from the code
choices.why: Lesson 9's function produces no drawing; it fails the build.

choices.text: It is cheaper to write than a deck of slides
choices.why: Cost is not the argument; a cheap drawing that drifts is still the antipattern.

choices.text: It breaks the build when the code stops obeying the rule
choices.why: Right: a diagram that cannot drift, because the disagreement shows up the same day.

prompt: "Payments subscribes to the delivery-proved event" should come with an owner and a date; a target with no first ___ is a wish.
hint: The unit of a path.

prompt: What separates the ivory tower from the PowerPoint architect?
hint: One is far from the code, the other from…

choices.text: The tower is separated from the people who live with the decisions
choices.why: Right: a tower can sit on accurate diagrams and still decide without asking anybody.

choices.text: The tower writes documents; the other draws slides
choices.why: The medium separates nothing; both can use either.

choices.text: The tower designs too much and the other too little
choices.why: Designing too much is overengineering, which is a property of the design rather than of the stance.

choices.text: The tower belongs to enterprise architects only
choices.why: Any level of architect can decide from a distance; lesson 4's levels are not the point.

prompt: Renata announces at the all-hands that, from next quarter, every new service is written in Kotlin. She asked nobody. The Driver team, whose backend is Python and who know no Kotlin, hears it there. Which antipattern, and what was the alternative?
hint: Who was asked before the decision?

choices.text: The gatekeeper; she should approve each new service individually instead
choices.why: Approving each one is the gatekeeper, not the cure for deciding without asking.

choices.text: The ivory tower; seek the teams' advice before deciding
choices.why: Right: the advice process brings the Driver team's constraint in before the decision.

choices.text: Overengineering; one language for every team is more than Carreto needs
choices.why: The issue is how the decision was taken, not the size of what is built.

choices.text: The absent architect; she should have left languages to each team
choices.why: A new language in production is the architect's row; the fault was deciding it alone, not deciding it.

prompt: An architect personally approves every design. 18 designs reach her in a month, and each waits 5 working days. How many working days of waiting does that add up to in the month?
hint: Designs times days each waits.

prompt: After an outage caused by a bad migration, Renata rules that every pull request touching a database schema needs her approval. Six weeks later, schema changes wait three days for her and teams split migrations to stay under her radar. What is the better answer?
hint: A gate in front of what matters, not in front of everything.

choices.text: Keep the rule, but add a second approver to halve the wait
choices.why: Two gatekeepers are a shorter queue, still in front of decisions that belong to the teams.

choices.text: Drop schema checks altogether, since the teams own their tables
choices.why: That swaps the gatekeeper for the absent architect; the risk that caused the outage is still there.

choices.text: Automate checkable rules in CI; review only shared data
choices.why: Right: machines check what they can, and her review is kept for what crosses team boundaries.

choices.text: Ask the teams to batch their migrations into one weekly review
choices.why: Batching moves the queue to one day a week; it still waits on her for decisions that are the team's.

prompt: Which of these are symptoms of the ivory tower? Choose all that apply.
hint: Distance from the people, not from the code.

choices.text: Standards arrive with no reason anybody can argue with
choices.why: Yes: lesson 9's reason and owner are missing.

choices.text: The forum is a broadcast whose questions change nothing
choices.why: Yes: the teams learn that the forum is theatre.

choices.text: A plugin system with one plugin
choices.why: That is a symptom of overengineering.

choices.text: Teams stop mentioning their workarounds
choices.why: Yes: the real architecture drifts away from the declared one, invisibly.

choices.text: Pull requests wait days for the architect's approval
choices.why: That is the gatekeeper: close to the teams, not far from them.

prompt: The lesson calls the gatekeeper the ivory tower moved to the ___: very close to the teams, and approving all they do.
hint: Where a gate stands.

prompt: How does the lesson define overengineering?
hint: Whose problem is being solved?

choices.text: Building for a problem you do not have
choices.why: Right: flexibility, capacity or generality nobody asked for, paid for every month.

choices.text: Writing more tests than the code needs
choices.why: Tests are not what the lesson discusses; the cost it counts is pieces to run, upgrade and understand.

choices.text: Using a technology the team has not used before
choices.why: New technology spent on an interesting problem is one symptom, but plenty of new technology meets a real need.

choices.text: Designing a system before the requirements are complete
choices.why: Lesson 2 asks for just enough design up front; waiting for complete requirements is a different mistake.

prompt: A review finds an interface with one class behind it, a plugin loader with one plugin, and a configuration flag set to the same value in every environment. These are symptoms of…
hint: Abstractions with one implementation.

choices.text: The absent architect, since nobody designed this
choices.why: Somebody designed a great deal here; the absent architect leaves too little design, not too much.

choices.text: The PowerPoint architect
choices.why: The code here exists and matches its design; the trouble is that the design is bigger than the need.

choices.text: Overengineering
choices.why: Right: generality built for a second case that has not arrived.

choices.text: A healthy design that keeps options open for the future
choices.why: A clear boundary keeps an option open for almost nothing; machinery for the second case pays the full price now.

prompt: A notification service was sized for 1,500 messages a second. The measured peak last year was 5 a second. How many times the measured peak was it sized for?
hint: Designed divided by measured.

prompt: Renata's imagined fiscal document engine was meant to cover future countries. Which alternative does the lesson recommend for the CT-e change?
hint: Boundary, not machinery.

choices.text: Build the engine for Brazil first, and add the other countries later
choices.why: That keeps the plugin machinery and its running costs, for a second case that has not arrived.

choices.text: Change the CT-e module behind a boundary, noting when to revisit
choices.why: Right: the likely change stays cheap, and a decision record names the signal that would justify more.

choices.text: Buy a third-party fiscal platform that covers South America
choices.why: Buying generality for countries Carreto does not operate in is the same overreach, paid to a supplier.

choices.text: Wait until expansion is approved before touching the CT-e code
choices.why: The new layout has a fixed regulatory date (lesson 13); the change cannot wait on a decision that may never come.

prompt: Three teams publish events three different ways, two services read each other's tables, and nobody can say who owns the drivers table. No one ever chose this. Which antipattern is it?
hint: A structure that happened by accident.

choices.text: The ivory tower
choices.why: A tower decides too much from too far; here nobody decided at all.

choices.text: Overengineering, because there are too many mechanisms
choices.why: The mechanisms are many because nobody chose one, not because somebody built for a future need.

choices.text: The gatekeeper
choices.why: A gatekeeper would have stopped these at the door; there was no door.

choices.text: The absent architect: accidental architecture, a big ball of mud
choices.why: Right: each local decision was sensible, and the sum is a structure nobody chose.

prompt: Put the steps of the lesson's alternative to oversizing a service in order.
hint: Number first, design second, proof third, the record last.
items: Ask for the measured peak and the expected growth
Design for that peak with an agreed margin
Prove the capacity with a load test
Record what was not built and what would trigger it
trap: Designing before asking for the number is how a quote service ends up sized for 2,000 requests a second.

prompt: Match each Carreto situation to the antipattern it shows.
hint: Distance, control, or size of the design.

pairs.left: the deck shows an event; the code polls an API every five minutes
a rule announced at the all-hands that no team was asked about
every new library needs the architect's signature
a rules engine for three countries in a company that operates in one

prompt: Kátia asks Renata whether Matching should cache driver profiles. Renata answers with a 30-page document describing a company-wide caching platform, which she presents to Tomás and nobody else. Matching ships its own small cache the next week. Which antipattern is closest, and what would the alternative have been?
hint: Who was the answer for, and who built anything?

choices.text: The gatekeeper; she should have let Matching decide without telling her
choices.why: She approved nothing and blocked nothing; the team went ahead without her answer.

choices.text: The absent architect; she should have written a decision record
choices.why: She was anything but absent; thirty pages is a great deal of presence aimed at the wrong reader.

choices.text: The PowerPoint architect; answer Kátia with her team, as a shippable step
choices.why: Right: a document for executives about a system nobody is building, while the real decision happens elsewhere.

choices.text: Overengineering above all; a shorter document focused on caching would have settled it
choices.why: The platform is oversized, but the deeper failure is that the drawing never met the code or the team.

prompt: The Tracking team proposes running its own Kafka cluster to receive truck positions, citing "future scale". Asked for numbers, it reports 8,000 trucks sending a position every 30 seconds, and a managed queue it already uses handling that load at a fifth of its capacity. What should Renata's review say?
hint: Lesson 12, count the pieces; lesson 5, the record.

choices.text: Approve it: positions are high-volume data and Kafka is built for that
choices.why: The measured load fits the existing queue five times over; the cluster is a new piece to run for no named need.

choices.text: Keep the managed queue, and record the load at which to revisit
choices.why: Right: design for the measured need with a margin, and write down the signal that would justify more.

choices.text: Ask Platform to build a company-wide streaming platform instead
choices.why: That answers overengineering with a bigger version of it.

choices.text: Leave it to Tracking, because the data is theirs
choices.why: A new broker in production is the architect's row in lesson 16's table; the team must be asked, and she answers for it.

prompt: The lesson maps each antipattern to lessons that prevent it. Which pairing is the one it gives for the gatekeeper?
hint: What replaces personal approval?

choices.text: Standards checked by machines, and the decision-rights table
choices.why: Right: lessons 9, 11 and 16. Judgement built into how teams decide rather than applied to each decision.

choices.text: Living documentation, and keeping on coding
choices.why: Those are lessons 8 and 15, which prevent the PowerPoint architect.

choices.text: Scenarios with numbers and simplifying
choices.why: Lessons 6 and 12 prevent overengineering.

choices.text: Gathering requirements and earned authority
choices.why: Lessons 7 and 3 prevent the ivory tower.
